bloks.name: STRAIGHT UP
bloks.title: Do You Have What It Takes to Be Early?
bloks.dek: When the crowd moves, step out.

body.text: Being early means having the courage to stand on a position, a truth, or a value—long before the room catches on.
Our primal instincts tell us to follow the pack to survive.
But you can flip that instinct into a counter-signal: when the crowd moves, step out.

body.cap: If you’re early, you might walk it alone.
body.alt: A lone figure walks through blue fog past the ruins of a collapsed city.

body.text: If you wait, you’ll always be dragged along by the warmth of the crowd’s sentiment.
If you recognize the moment, you give yourself a chance to lead and think for yourself—seeing where your true allies really are.
Do you have what it takes to be early?

bloks.name: WORD MEME
bloks.title: To Mog or Get Mogged in a Moggy Mog World
bloks.dek: How a forum acronym became Gen Z and Gen Alpha’s favorite brag.

body.text: “Mog” (or “mogging”) is a popular Gen Z/Alpha slang term meaning to outshine, outperform, or appear superior to someone else, particularly in attractiveness, fashion, or physical appearance. Originating from the acronym AMOG (“Alpha Male of the Group”), it is often used on social media to describe dominating others or being “shown up” in photos.
—the internet
Mog is genuinely one of my favorite terms. At first, it’s an odd expression. It feels like wet laundry out of the mouth.
But with time, and taking notice of its cultural rise, the embrace of the word becomes real.

body.alt: A Times Square billboard reads “Mog or get Mogged” as people on the street look up.

body.text: Somewhere around the early 2000s, before the word knew it existed, the term “AMOG” (Alpha Male of the Group) sprouted up as a way to call out which guy in a group was the leader.
Certain words and expressions have a way of growing beneath the surface, through situational use, and becoming repurposed.
And that’s exactly what happened with mog by the early 2020s, as it ascended through the cultural ranks, picked up mostly by Gen Z and Gen Alpha as everyday slang.

body.alt: A cartoon girl in round sunglasses wears a T-shirt that reads “it’s a mog or get mogged world.”

body.text: If you got mogged, you were shown up, outshined, got beat or outclassed.
If you did the mogging, you shredded the competition or picked up some kind of life-win—in some cases when others doubted.
It’s an emphatic way to brag, describe triumph or admit defeat.
Unexpected Twist: Mog Glasses
Enter Mog Coin in 2023, a crypto token built around a community of lovers of the term itself — then given a mascot to go with it.

body.cap: The Mog Coin logo
body.alt: The Mog Coin logo: a laughing cat wearing pixelated rainbow glasses.

body.text: The Mog Glasses have become a symbol and meme unto themselves. And the visual memification of mog — the glasses, the term, and the Mog Cat character — has been blazing its own path ever since. It’s an uncontrollable internet meme that spills out of the screen and into real-life conversation.
Which is how we got here, getting mogged by mog itself.

body.alt: Animated Mog Cat meme with pixel glasses.
Anime-style cat girl in rainbow pixel glasses with the words “it’s a mog or get mogged world.”

bloks.name: BEHIND THE REEL
bloks.title: 50 Years Later, Still Mad as Hell
bloks.dek: One person, the right tools, and Network’s most famous scene remade with AI.

body.text: The cinema classic Network is one of those movies that hasn’t quite had the moment it truly deserves. Not because it wasn’t great but because its warning rang so true, people tend to avoid it.
The movie held a mirror to society, and since that moment it has existed inside the broader popular consciousness, waiting to be unearthed again.
That’s what the AI remake of this iconic “I’m mad as hell” scene captures—raw, urgent, and unnervingly current.

bloks.name: UNDERGROUND
bloks.title: Scipher Punx’ Dystopique — the Just-in-Case Album
bloks.dek: The year is 2113. An insurance policy against a reality that feels increasingly near.

body.text: The year is 2113. The incremental control of society has taken full form.
We live in ghettoized cities, saturated with cameras, programmable money units, and a world where every aspect of life has been restricted by way of calculations and monetization.
Scipher Punx is an insurance policy against a reality that feels increasingly near.
The Dystopique album channels everyday discontent into instrumental and lyrical rebellion.

The album’s tenor clamors like sound waves that ricochet off a city’s concrete corporate buildings—the ones with the reflective windows you can’t see through. It reeks of CCTVs, self-preservation, and a fractured society.
It suggests that our drive to self-automate the world led straight to our own entrapment—placing us squarely in the middle of it.
As a listener, prepare for a mashup of drum & bass, hip-hop, house, trap, and glitch, driven by wobbly bass and subterranean rumbles.
Quick Album Run-Through

It opens with “Cyphergrid Collapse,” where you might as well be in a high-speed chase from authorities on a party bus. The next two tracks, “Protocol Breach” and “Terminal Velocity,” extend that frantic energy in their own ways.

body.cap: Inspired by “Blackout”
body.alt: An electrical tower against a dark, stormy sky, edged in neon.

body.text: “Blackout” delivers the first (short) lyrical display, signaling readiness for a grid collapse. The only question: was it triggered by the elites, or the population themselves? Either way, the message is clear—if the power goes out, the sub-citizen plebs are prepared.

body.cap: The “Blackout” bonus visual. Watch on Instagram.
body.alt: Scipher Punx “Blackout” bonus visual on Instagram

body.text: “Neon Wasteland” is an ode to a future-facing rap love ballad. The hook:

“Neon wasteland, neon wasteland
We’re the only real thing in a fake land
Neon wasteland, neon wasteland
Encrypted love, they can’t understand”
It’s followed by “Encrypted Memories,” an early-century-style electronic ballad about hiding your true self in an encrypted digital space. She sings:

“The underground is where we trade
The only thoughts that haven’t frayed
Pure experience, unrefined
The last rebellion of the mind”

From there, acting like an intermission, the album shifts into the cinematic slowdown of the spoken-word “Ghost Protocol.” At track nine comes the abrasive, industrial-rap “He’s—comp—mised,” shadowing a man hunted for “breathing unmonitored air” in a city that’s a “circuit board prison.” Listen closely to see what happens.

body.alt: A hooded man runs down a graffiti alley through red laser beams under a sign that reads COMPROMISED.

body.text: The penultimate track, “Zero Day,” is a rare feel-good moment: a secret speakeasy on the 13th floor of an unmarked, abandoned corporate tower with thin, slit windows. It gives the people a moment to reflect on what life was before it grew so messy and untenable. Sung like a chilled-out Johnny Cash over downtempo drums, it’s a chance to remember.
The album closes with “ShadowNet (So You Wanted This Future),” forcing us to look in the mirror. It suggests we got exactly what we asked for:

“You wanted convenience
Total access, seamless experience
Now the algorithms know
Every move before you do”
If This Ever Happens

So just in case we find ourselves in a world where governments overreach, the population at large is reduced to wage slaves, our entire society is controlled by algorithms and automation, we’ve been stripped of our fundamental humanity, and forced by calculated submission to surrender our time and energy on society’s terms rather than retaining any semblance of our own agency—this album is for those moments.
Just in case…if that ever were to happen 😜😉😜😉😜
Enjoy.

bloks.name: MUSIC FLOW
bloks.title: What’s a Portishead?
bloks.dek: Out of the reference and into the source.

body.text: Last issue we went into a story inside a story when we talked about a TV show that featured a cover of a song by the band Portishead.
This issue, we step out of the reference and into the source.
Portishead’s arrival is the ultimate “you had to be there” moment.
At its core, it’s Beth Gibbons and her eerily beautiful voice singing about love, loss, womanhood, and depression.

The sound was forged alongside Geoff Barrow, the producer and sonic architect layering hip-hop samples and analog textures, and Adrian Utley, whose live guitar work took that textured electronic fabric and humanized it.
Before the trio even locked in, it was local DJ Andy Smith’s crate-digging and shared record collection that supplied the foundational loops and cinematic source material they built on.

body.cap: Geoff Barrow (background) and Beth Gibbons in the early ’90s. Photograph: Mark McNulty/Retna
body.alt: Black-and-white photo of Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons sitting against a metal shutter.

body.text: Portishead is like a first love. A band that gave us permission to feel, at a time when being “not okay” wasn’t considered cool. They didn’t just crack the door open to peek at our emotions, they created a timeless portal to walk into and sit in as long as you needed.
We sometimes say artists are “ahead of their time.” But that’s not quite accurate here—because nothing ever actually caught up. And how could it?
In a modern culture becoming more cookie-cutter by the day—shaped by online social algorithms and dwindling originality—Portishead remains the ultimate singular effort.
Words struggle to pin it down, but I’ll try: downtempo electronic drums, cinematic samples, live instrumentation, and Gibbons’ haunted vocals fused into something starkly original.
At the time, it felt like a preamble for a new musical era to come—except nothing ever did.
You could argue Portishead helped birth downtempo electronic. But that still misses what the band actually was: cinematic, emotional, dark, and fiercely, soulfully authentic.
They dialed into a frequency we’d never heard before—and time has proven we’ll likely never hear anything like it again. That’s why it’s guarded like a protected world treasure.
So what’s a Portishead? It’s a quiet town eight miles west of Bristol, from which they came. And now it lives in history as something entirely different.
Better than a James Bond soundtrack:

bloks.name: NOW PLAYING
bloks.title: Robert Downey Jr.’s Masterclass Inside Sherlock Holmes
bloks.dek: We watch the spectacle, but miss the mastery.

body.text: The role of Sherlock Holmes has been played for over a century. Robert Downey Jr. couldn’t just inherit it.
He had to rebuild it through quiet, deliberate choices: how he thinks, how he drinks, how he holds a pause, how he treats every moment like a chess match.

body.cap: Sherlock Holmes (2009). Watch on YouTube.
body.alt: Scene from Sherlock Holmes (2009)

body.text: It’s a masterclass in control. And like the best craft, it’s hiding in plain sight. We watch the spectacle, but miss the mastery.
